## I. Policy Architecture: The Core Tension

### The Fundamental Problem

The company faces a three-axis tension:

**Axis 1: Visibility vs. Autonomy.** In some cultural contexts—particularly in high-trust, results-oriented environments—the amount of time an employee spends at a desk or in an office is irrelevant. What matters is whether the work gets done. In other contexts, physical presence signals commitment, diligence, and respect. An employee who leaves the office at 5:00 PM in a high-presence culture may be perceived as a poor performer regardless of output quality. Compressed weeks and remote work, in this context, are not liberating; they are threatening.

**Axis 2: Generational Expectation vs. Established Norm.** Younger employees in markets where four-day week pilots have been publicized—particularly in Northern Europe, parts of Asia-Pacific, and English-speaking markets with strong labor movements—view flexibility as a baseline expectation. In other markets, employees who have built careers on visible dedication may view flexibility policies as benefiting younger employees at their expense, or as an implicit criticism of the career-long sacrifices they made.

**Axis 3: Legal Mandate vs. Operational Desire.** Right-to-disconnect laws in some markets legally restrict after-hours communication; in others, no such laws exist and after-hours availability is culturally expected or contractually implied. Four-day work week pilots have produced legislation in some jurisdictions while remaining experimental in others. The company cannot apply the most restrictive standard globally without constraining operations, but it cannot ignore legal minimums in any market.

### Design Principle

This policy resolves the tension through **regional calibration within global boundaries**, not through compromise across all markets. The company will not choose between a generous policy that fails in high-presence markets and a restrictive policy that fails in autonomy-seeking markets. Instead, it will establish a range of acceptable configurations, each compliant with local law and adapted to local culture, that share common philosophical commitments.

This policy applies to all full-time and part-time employees of the company and its wholly owned subsidiaries across its twelve country offices. It does not apply to:

- Contractors and contingent workers, who are governed by their own engagement terms and applicable local law
- Employees in probationary periods, who are subject to the Modified Eligibility provisions in Section VIII
- Seconded employees, who remain subject to the policies of their home country office

Performance is evaluated on the basis of **delivered outputs, collaboration effectiveness, and professional development**, not on hours logged, physical presence, or visible busyness. Managers in all markets are accountable for evaluating performance on these terms, and performance management systems must be calibrated accordingly.

**What this requires globally:**

- All job descriptions include outcome-based success criteria that are specific, measurable, and independent of attendance or location
- Performance reviews assess outputs against agreed objectives, not presence or hours
- Promotion criteria are explicitly tied to delivery, collaboration quality, and professional growth—not office attendance, availability outside hours, or visible effort
- Managers are trained and held accountable for evaluating performance on outcome criteria, and this competency is assessed in manager performance reviews

**Performance management mechanisms:**

- Quarterly objectives are defined in terms of deliverables, not activities
- 360-degree feedback includes questions about collaboration quality, not availability patterns
- Calibration sessions include a structured review of whether remote or flexible employees receive equivalent recognition to on-site peers
- Compensation decisions (merit increases, bonuses, equity awards) are audited for correlation with flexibility arrangement type; any statistically significant disparity triggers a review of the decision-making process

- Legal review of all regional policy variants before implementation, conducted by local counsel in each jurisdiction
- Annual legal compliance audit for each country office, with findings reported to the Global Flexibility Working Group
- A legal compliance matrix maintained centrally and updated within 60 days of any material change in legislation
- Clear escalation path for employees who believe their rights are being violated, operating independently of the normal management chain to ensure protection against retaliation
- Ongoing legislative monitoring through a designated legal resource in each market

### Principle 3: Team Accountability

Individual flexibility exists within the context of team obligations. Flexibility is not unlimited discretion—it is structured autonomy exercised within team commitments, client service requirements, and collaborative workflows.

**What this requires globally:**

- Team-level agreements that define collaboration windows, overlap hours, and meeting attendance expectations, developed collaboratively by each team within global parameters
- Clear identification of role-specific requirements (client-facing hours, time-zone coverage, availability during core business hours) before any flexibility arrangement is approved
- Team accountability mechanisms that make flexibility visible as a collective arrangement, not an individual perk
- Manager authority to set team-level parameters within the global framework and to revoke flexibility arrangements that systematically undermine team obligations, subject to appeal

Flexible work arrangements are only as effective as the managers who implement them. Managers who cannot set clear expectations, provide constructive feedback, manage performance across distance, and support team collaboration in a flexible environment will undermine any policy, regardless of its design.

**What this requires globally:**

- Manager certification program, completed before teams under a manager's supervision are eligible for Tier 2, Tier 3, or Tier 4 arrangements
- Ongoing manager development on outcome-based performance management, delivered annually
- Manager performance evaluation incorporating team flexibility management effectiveness as a rated competency
- Resources (training, coaching, peer support) for managers operating in mixed-attendance or fully-remote teams, available on demand
- Manager certification covers: outcome-based objective setting, performance conversations without presence cues, managing distributed teams, preventing proximity bias, handling flexibility exceptions, right-to-disconnect enforcement, and cultural awareness for managing cross-border teams

### Principle 5: Equity, Not Equality

The policy aims for equitable access to flexibility across demographics, roles, and seniority levels—not identical treatment, which would be neither equitable nor operationally sensible. Certain roles cannot be performed flexibly (facilities staff, hardware lab technicians, security personnel); the policy addresses these role-specific constraints directly rather than ignoring them.

Equitable access means that the barriers to flexibility are objective (role requirements, legal constraints, operational needs) rather than discretionary (manager preference, cultural norm, seniority-based privilege). The company monitors uptake and outcome data to identify where discretionary barriers are distorting equitable access.

### Tier 3: Compressed or Reduced Work Week

**Core provision:** Employees may restructure their working week to concentrate standard hours into fewer days, or may reduce total hours with corresponding compensation adjustment. Tier 3 requires formal application, manager recommendation, HR approval, and a six-month trial with defined outcome metrics.

| **Four-day week (compressed: standard hours in four days)** | Work standard weekly hours Monday–Thursday, with Friday off | Available where legally permitted and operationally feasible for the role. | **Four-day week (reduced: 32 hours at 80% compensation)** | Work 32 hours (80% of standard) for 80% of base compensation | Available where legally permitted. Requires explicit manager and HR approval and a six-month trial with review. Benefits and equity vesting pro-rated accordingly. |
| **Nine-day fortnight** | Work standard hours across nine days every two weeks, with every other Friday off | Available in most markets. Appeals to markets where employees appreciate variety over rigid schedule changes. |
| **Job share** | Two employees share a full-time role, each working part-time | Available globally. Requires role suitability assessment, formal job-share agreement, and configuration review to ensure coverage. |

**Compensation principles for Tier 3:**

- **Compressed (full hours, fewer days):** No change to base compensation. The employee works the same total hours in fewer days. This is the preferred option for four-day weeks because it maintains pay equity.
- **Reduced (fewer hours, proportionally less pay):** Compensation is reduced proportionally to hours. This is appropriate when the reduction is substantial and sustained, not merely seasonal.
- **Proportionality review:** If a reduced-hours arrangement is combined with a role change (e.g., moving from a senior role to a reduced-scope role), compensation adjustment may exceed the proportional hours reduction. HR determines this on a case-by-case basis.
- **Benefits:** Benefits that are tied to hours (e.g., accrual-based leave) are adjusted proportionally. Benefits that are not tied to hours (health insurance, equity) remain unchanged unless legally required otherwise.

**Eligibility criteria for Tier 3:**

- Minimum 12 months of service (excluding probationary period)
- Current performance rating of "meets expectations" or above
- Role categorized as Category B (Collaborative, Outcome-Oriented) or specifically approved by HR on exception
- Manager certification completed
- Team coverage plan documented and approved
- Client impact assessment completed (for client-facing roles)
- Trial objectives and metrics agreed in writing before commencement

**What the evidence tells us about four-day weeks:**

Global pilots conducted between 2022 and 2025—including Iceland's national trial (2015–2019), the UK's largest four-day week pilot (2022, 61 companies, 2,900 employees), Unilever's partnership with the Productivity Institute (2023), and pilot programs in Australia, Canada, Japan, and South Africa—consistently demonstrated that:

1. **Role fit is the strongest predictor of success.** Roles with clear output metrics, controlled meeting loads, and limited real-time client demands showed the strongest results. Software development, engineering, internal operations, and analytical roles performed well. Client-facing sales, professional services, and roles with high crisis management demands showed more variable results.

2. **Process improvement is a prerequisite, not an accompaniment.** The most successful pilots required teams to eliminate or restructure low-value work alongside hour reduction. Simply compressing the same workload into fewer hours produced burnout, quality degradation, or informal after-hours work that defeated the purpose.

3. **Collaborative design outperforms top-down mandates.** Teams that designed their own arrangements—deciding which day to take off, how to cover meetings, how to restructure workflows—consistently outperformed those receiving standardized prescriptions.

4. **Sustained results require cultural change, not just schedule change.** Many pilots showed initial enthusiasm that faded as the novelty wore off and the underlying work culture reasserted itself. Organizations that treated four-day weeks as a scheduling change alone had higher reversion rates than those that treated it as part of a broader cultural shift.

5. **The 100-80-100 model (100% of pay for 80% of time in exchange for 100% of productivity) showed the strongest results in terms of employee wellbeing and retention, though revenue impact was mixed.**

**Regional calibration examples:**

Tier 3 should be presented as an earned privilege tied to team performance and individual track record, not an entitlement.
- *Spain:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible and supported by Spain's progressive labor reforms. - *Germany:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible as a working time arrangement. - *France:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible. - *UAE:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible under UAE Labour Law. - *Japan:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible. Japan's Labor Standards Act caps the working week at 40 hours. - *South Korea:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible under the Labor Standards Act (40-hour work week limit, with a 52-hour upper limit including overtime). Younger employees in tech and startup environments have expressed strong interest, but uptake is likely to be gradual.

- Every team on Tier 3 arrangements must have coverage during the reduced employee's working day. This is the manager's responsibility to arrange, not the employee's.

- Coverage arrangements are reviewed at each trial checkpoint.

**Core provision:** Employees may work entirely remotely with no required in-office presence, subject to periodic in-person requirements for strategic purposes.

- Remote workers in a foreign country may create a **permanent establishment** for the company, triggering corporate tax obligations
- Remote workers may create **employment law obligations** in their country of residence that differ from their country of employment
- Remote workers may become subject to **social security contributions** in their country of residence
- The company may be required to **withhold taxes** according to the rules of the remote worker's country of residence

- Demonstration of effective independent collaboration

   - Expected response times for different types of communication during working hours (e.g., email: within 4 hours during core hours; instant messages: within 1 hour during core hours; project management tools: within one working day)

# Global Flexible Work Policy Framework

## A Culturally Adaptive, Legally Compliant, and Operationally Sustainable Policy for a Global Software Company

---

## Executive Summary

The premise of this policy is straightforward: a one-size-fits-all approach to flexible work will fail in a global organization where employees in one market experience compressed weeks as liberation and employees in another market experience the same arrangement as career-limiting or disrespectful. The challenge is not merely logistical—it is cultural, legal, and managerial. What "flexibility" means, what "commitment" signals, and what "visibility" earns differs systematically across the twelve country offices in ways that reflect not employee preference alone but deeply held beliefs about professional reciprocity, organizational loyalty, and the social contract between employer and employee.

This policy does not resolve those differences by imposing a single definition. Instead, it establishes a **global framework of principles and boundaries** within which each regional office adapts the policy to its legal environment, cultural context, and operational requirements. The framework prioritizes outcome-based performance management, legally compliant working-time arrangements, and managerial capability as the primary enablers of sustainable flexibility—not technology, not office design, and not corporate edict.

The policy is designed for implementation from 2026 onward, in an environment where **right-to-disconnect legislation has proliferated unevenly** across the company's markets, four-day work week pilots have generated mixed but instructive results, and employee expectations—particularly among younger cohorts—have shifted substantially toward flexibility as a non-negotiable employment condition.

## I. Policy Architecture: The Core Tension

### The Fundamental Problem

The company faces a three-axis tension:

**Axis 1: Visibility vs. Autonomy.** In some cultural contexts—particularly in high-trust, results-oriented environments—the amount of time an employee spends at a desk or in an office is irrelevant. What matters is whether the work gets done. In other contexts, physical presence signals commitment, diligence, and respect. An employee who leaves the office at 5:00 PM in a high-presence culture may be perceived as a poor performer regardless of output quality. Compressed weeks and remote work, in this context, are not liberating; they are threatening.

**Axis 2: Generational Expectation vs. Established Norm.** Younger employees in markets where four-day week pilots have been publicized—particularly in Northern Europe, parts of Asia-Pacific, and English-speaking markets with strong labor movements—view flexibility as a baseline expectation. In other markets, employees who have built careers on visible dedication may view flexibility policies as benefiting younger employees at their expense, or as an implicit criticism of the career-long sacrifices they made.

**Axis 3: Legal Mandate vs. Operational Desire.** Right-to-disconnect laws in some markets legally restrict after-hours communication; in others, no such laws exist and after-hours availability is culturally expected or contractually implied. Four-day work week pilots have produced legislation in some jurisdictions while remaining experimental in others. The company cannot apply the most restrictive standard globally without constraining operations, but it cannot ignore legal minimums in any market.

### Design Principle

This policy resolves the tension through **regional calibration within global boundaries**, not through compromise across all markets. The company will not choose between a generous policy that fails in high-presence markets and a restrictive policy that fails in autonomy-seeking markets. Instead, it will establish a range of acceptable configurations, each compliant with local law and adapted to local culture, that share common philosophical commitments.

## II. Global Principles

These principles apply in all twelve country offices without exception. They are not negotiable at the regional level, but their implementation is.

### Principle 1: Outcome Primacy

Performance is evaluated on the basis of **delivered outputs, collaboration effectiveness, and professional development**, not on hours logged, physical presence, or visible busyness. Managers in all markets are accountable for evaluating performance on these terms, and performance management systems must be calibrated accordingly.

**What this requires globally:**

- All job descriptions include outcome-based success criteria
- Performance reviews assess outputs against agreed objectives, not presence
- Promotion criteria are explicitly tied to delivery and collaboration, not office attendance
- Managers are trained and held accountable for outcome-based management

**Implementation note:** This principle is non-negotiable globally because it is the foundation of fairness. A policy that promises flexibility but evaluates on presence is not a flexible policy—it is a trap.

### Principle 2: Legal Floor

No regional policy may fall below the legal minimum standards of the relevant jurisdiction. This includes working time limits, mandatory rest periods, right-to-disconnect protections, overtime rules, and notice requirements for schedule changes.

**What this requires globally:**

- Legal review of all regional policy variants before implementation
- Annual legal compliance audit for each country office
- A legal compliance matrix maintained centrally and updated as legislation evolves
- Clear escalation path for employees who believe their rights are being violated

### Principle 3: Team Accountability

Individual flexibility exists within the context of team obligations. Flexibility is not unlimited discretion—it is structured autonomy exercised within team commitments, client service requirements, and collaborative workflows.

**What this requires globally:**

- Team-level agreements that define collaboration windows, overlap hours, and meeting attendance expectations
- Clear identification of role-specific requirements (client-facing hours, time-zone coverage, availability during trading hours)
- Team accountability mechanisms that make flexibility visible as a collective arrangement, not an individual perk
- Manager authority to set team-level parameters within the global framework

### Principle 4: Managerial Capability as Prerequisite

Flexible work arrangements are only as effective as the managers who implement them. Managers who cannot set clear expectations, provide constructive feedback, manage performance across distance, and support team collaboration in a flexible environment will undermine any policy, regardless of its design.

**What this requires globally:**

- Manager certification program on flexible work management before teams are eligible for certain policy tiers
- Ongoing manager development on outcome-based performance management
- Manager performance evaluation incorporating team flexibility management effectiveness
- Resources (training, coaching, peer support) for managers operating in mixed-attendance or fully-remote teams

### Principle 5: Equity, Not Equality

The policy aims for equitable access to flexibility across demographics, roles, and seniority levels—not identical treatment, which would be neither equitable nor operationally sensible. Certain roles cannot be performed flexibly (facilities staff, hardware lab technicians); the policy addresses these role-specific constraints directly rather than ignoring them.

## III. The Policy Options: Four Tiers

Rather than offering a single "flexible work policy," this framework defines **four tiers of flexibility**, each with associated eligibility criteria, structural requirements, and regional customization parameters. Not all tiers are available in all markets; availability depends on role suitability, legal compliance, and regional adoption readiness.

### Tier 1: Flexible Hours (Default)

**Core provision:** Employees may vary their start and end times within a defined core window, subject to team collaboration requirements.

| Parameter | Standard Configuration | Regional Customization Range |
|-----------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| **Core hours (all employees must be available)** | 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM local time | 9:00 AM – 2:00 PM to 11:00 AM – 4:00 PM (adjusted for local norms) |
| **Working day length** | Standard full-time hours (e.g., 8 hours) | May be reduced to 7.5 hours with manager approval in markets where cultural norms support shorter days |
| **Right-to-disconnect boundary** | After 6:00 PM local time, no expectation of response unless on-call | Legally mandated boundaries take precedence; where no law exists, 6:00 PM is the default |
| **Location** | Office-based; no remote work requirement or restriction under this tier | — |
| **Meeting attendance** | Expected during core hours; may decline non-essential meetings outside core hours | — |

**Regional calibration examples:**

- *Germany:* Core window adjusted to 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM. Works council consultation required for any core-hour modification. Right-to-disconnect expectation is legally recognized even without specific legislation; after-hours communication should be exceptional and justified.
- *Japan:* Core window may be extended to 11:00 AM – 4:00 PM given cultural expectations around arrival time. However, right-to-disconnect boundaries are weaker; cultural expectation of availability after hours should be managed through team agreements, not assumed.
- *Brazil:* Core window of 9:00 AM – 3:00 PM allows for the common 6-hour workday followed by personal time. Right-to-disconnect expectation applies; Brazil's Constitution establishes limits on employer demands outside working hours.
- *Singapore:* Core window of 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM; no statutory right-to-disconnect. Team norms govern after-hours communication, which tends to be higher than in European markets. Managers should explicitly negotiate after-hours expectations rather than assuming availability.

**Eligibility:** All full-time and part-time employees in roles that do not require physical presence at a specific location or shift coverage are eligible for Tier 1. This is the baseline policy; all other tiers are enhancements.

---

### Tier 2: Flexible Location (Hybrid)

**Core provision:** Employees may work from home or another location for a defined portion of the working week, with required in-office days for collaboration.

| Parameter | Standard Configuration | Regional Customization Range |
|-----------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| **In-office days per week** | 3 days | 2–4 days, depending on regional labor law, cultural norms, and role requirements |
| **Required collaboration days** | Tuesday and Thursday (or equivalent team days) | May be modified based on team timezone spread and client coverage needs |
| **Remote location** | Employee's country of employment (standard); cross-border remote requires separate authorization | — |
| **Equipment and expenses** | Company-provided equipment; stipend for home internet and electricity | Market-indexed stipend; may be omitted in markets where equipment is provided in kind |
| **Right-to-disconnect boundary** | Applies equally to remote and office work | — |

**Regional calibration examples:**

- *United Kingdom:* Tier 2 eligible. Right-to-disconnect is not yet legislated but is established as an acas recommendation. Three-day office expectation is consistent with market norms; younger employees seeking four-day weeks would need to progress to Tier 3.
- *Australia:* Tier 2 eligible. Fair Work Act governs flexible work requests; employees with caring responsibilities or medical conditions have a right to request specific arrangements. The policy should be positioned as meeting or exceeding these rights.
- *South Korea:* Tier 2 may need to be calibrated carefully. Despite stated preferences for flexibility, cultural expectations around office presence are strong, particularly in hierarchical organizations. A three-day office expectation may be perceived as insufficient in the current cultural environment, while a five-day expectation will drive attrition among younger employees. Mid-range calibration (three days, with explicit senior leader modeling) is recommended.
- *India:* Tier 2 eligible with four-day in-office expectation for most roles given client timezone requirements (US and Europe client coverage often requires overlap hours). Right-to-disconnect is not legally mandated. Tier 2 in India should be framed as generous relative to market norms to manage expectations.

**Equity note for Tier 2:** Hybrid work creates a two-tier experience within the same office. Employees who live close to the office and employees who live far from it experience Tier 2 differently. The company should:

- Index in-office day requirements to office location, not role seniority
- Provide co-working space access for employees who live far from the primary office
- Ensure that career advancement decisions are not influenced by an employee's physical presence in ways that contradict Principle 1

### Tier 3: Compressed or Reduced Work Week

**Core provision:** Employees may restructure their working week to concentrate standard hours into fewer days, or may reduce total hours with corresponding compensation adjustment.

| Option | Configuration | Regional Availability |
|--------|--------------|----------------------|
| **Four-day week (standard hours in four days)** | Work standard weekly hours Monday–Thursday, with Friday off | Available where legally permitted and operationally feasible for the role. Not available in markets where five-day presence is legally mandated for the role category. |
| **Four-day week (reduced hours)** | Work 32 hours (80% of standard) for 80% of compensation | Available where legally permitted. Requires explicit manager and HR approval and a six-month trial with review. |
| **Nine-day fortnight** | Work standard hours across nine days every two weeks, with every other Friday off | Available in most markets as an alternative to full four-day weeks. Appeals to markets where employees appreciate variety over rigid schedule changes. |
| **Job share (reduced hours)** | Two employees share a full-time role, each working part-time | Available globally. Requires role suitability assessment and formal job-share agreement. |

**Important distinction:** Four-day week pilots conducted globally between 2022 and 2025 produced varied results. The company's approach incorporates these lessons:

- **Outcome fidelity:** Not all four-day week implementations maintained productivity. Roles with high meeting loads, client-facing requirements, or interdependent workflows showed less success. Eligibility for Tier 3 should be role-assessed, not tenure-assessed.
- **Revenue generation vs. support functions:** Commercial and client-facing roles may have more difficulty sustaining four-day weeks due to client expectations in markets where four-day weeks are not the norm. Tier 3 may be more readily available in engineering, product, and internal support functions than in client services.
- **Trial periods:** The most successful pilots used structured trials with defined success metrics. The company adopts a **six-month trial with outcome review** as the standard approach for Tier 3 arrangements.
- **Manager buy-in:** Tier 3 arrangements that are imposed top-down without manager engagement consistently underperform those developed collaboratively with teams.

**Regional calibration examples:**

- *UK:* Four-day week is legally available. Several pilots have been conducted by major employers. Tier 3 should be presented as an earned privilege tied to team performance and individual track record, not an entitlement. Market expectation is that four-day weeks maintain full output.
- *Spain:* Spain's right-to-disconnect framework is emerging. Four-day weeks are legally permissible. However, the culture of presenteeism in some Spanish workplaces is strong; Tier 3 rollout should include senior leader participation and explicit communication that reduced presence does not signal reduced commitment.
- *Germany:* Works council (Betriebsrat) involvement is legally required for any change in working time arrangements. Tier 3 in Germany requires works council negotiation at the Betriebsvereinbarung level, not merely manager approval. Timeline for implementation is longer than in markets without co-determination requirements.
- *France:* France has the most robust right-to-disconnect framework in the EU (the Loi Graveault of 2017). After-hours work communication is legally restricted. Tier 3 in France is compatible with this framework; four-day weeks require the standard legal working time ceiling (35 hours/week or negotiated collective agreement terms). Managerial staff (cadres) on forfait jours arrangements have additional flexibility.
- *Philippines:* Tier 3 is legally available but culturally complex. "Bayanihan" (community solidarity) cultural values can create pressure to work longer hours even when formal arrangements permit shorter weeks. Right-to-disconnect is not legislated. Tier 3 should be accompanied by explicit team agreements that prevent social pressure from undermining the formal arrangement.
- *United Arab Emirates:* Tier 3 is legally permissible under UAE Labour Law, which permits reduced working hours during Ramadan and has provisions for part-time arrangements. However, the culture of visible presence is strong in the Gulf region, and clients in the region may expect availability. Tier 3 is best suited to roles with limited client interaction. Where client-facing roles are considered, explicit client communication about availability changes is required.

**Managerial coverage requirements for Tier 3:**

- Every team on Tier 3 arrangements must have coverage during the reduced employee's absence. This is the manager's responsibility to arrange, not the employee's.
- Tier 3 arrangements that leave critical functions uncovered are not approved.
- Where coverage cannot be arranged, Tier 3 is not available for that role until coverage is resolved.

### Tier 4: Remote-First (Full Flexibility)

**Core provision:** Employees may work entirely remotely with no required in-office presence, subject to periodic in-person requirements for strategic purposes.

| Parameter | Configuration |
|-----------|--------------|
| **Location** | Employee's country of employment; cross-border remote requires separate international remote work agreement |
| **In-person requirements** | Minimum 4 weeks per year for team strategic planning, culture events, or mandatory in-person activities |
| **Equipment** | Company-provided equipment; enhanced home office stipend |
| **Right-to-disconnect** | Legally mandated boundaries apply; where no law exists, the policy default applies |
| **Eligibility** | Role-suitability assessed; manager approval; HR review; six-month trial period |

**Regional calibration notes:**

- Tier 4 is the most complex to implement due to the interaction between employment law, tax implications, social security contributions, and corporate presence requirements. In many countries, a foreign company employing a remote worker creates a "permanent establishment" risk that the company must evaluate.
- **Tier 4 is not available in all twelve offices.** Availability is determined on a country-by-country basis after legal and tax review.
- Countries where Tier 4 is likely available with minimal legal complexity: UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia (with Fair Work compliance), Netherlands, Sweden.
- Countries where Tier 4 requires significant legal review or is inadvisable due to permanent establishment risk: Japan, South Korea, India, UAE, Singapore.
- Countries where Tier 4 is legally complex but potentially manageable: Germany (works council negotiation required), France (cadres on forfait jours may be eligible), Brazil (employment law complexity, tax implications).

**Tier 4 is not a right.** It is an earned arrangement that requires:

- Successful completion of a Tier 2 or Tier 3 arrangement
- Consistent delivery against outcome-based performance criteria
- Demonstration of effective independent collaboration
- Manager recommendation
- HR and legal review

## IV. Right-to-Disconnect Protocol

Right-to-disconnect laws have proliferated unevenly across the company's markets. The company adopts the following protocol to ensure compliance while maintaining operational effectiveness.

### Legal Compliance Matrix (Illustrative)

| Country | Right-to-Disconnect Status (2026) | Policy Implication |
|---------|----------------------------------|-------------------|
| **France** | Legally mandated (Loi Graveault, 2017; strengthened 2024) | Mandatory. After-hours work communication must be exceptional and justified. All employees on electronic communication tools must be informed of their right to disconnect. |
| **Italy** | Legally mandated (Law No. 81/2017 for smart workers) | Mandatory for employees on formal smart working agreements. Company must establish specific protocols. |
| **Spain** | Emerging legislation; strong labor court precedent | Must be included in collective agreements. Policy should align with emerging legal standards. |
| **Ireland** | Code of Practice (not legislation, but legally relevant) | Company should follow the code; deviation creates legal risk. |
| **Belgium** | Legally mandated (2022) | After-hours communication must be justified and proportionate. Works council must be consulted. |
| **Germany** | Not separately legislated; embedded in working time law and co-determination rights | Works council can negotiate right-to-disconnect provisions. Recommended to adopt policy voluntarily to stay ahead of legislation. |
| **Netherlands** | Not separately legislated; labor court precedent favors employees | Voluntary policy recommended; strong cultural expectation of work-life separation. |
| **Australia** | Not separately legislated; Fair Work Act general protections apply | No mandatory legal requirement, but after-hours contact should be reasonable. Policy should include reasonable contact guidelines. |
| **UK** | Not legislated; introduced as a potential reform | No legal requirement, but voluntary adoption is recommended given cultural momentum and employee expectations. |
| **Japan** | Not legislated; "mental health" framework imposes implicit obligations | Voluntary policy strongly recommended. Cultural pressure for after-hours availability is high; explicit policy is necessary to counter it. |
| **Singapore** | Not legislated; Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangements recommend but do not mandate | No legal requirement. Policy should set internal expectations that exceed mere compliance. |
| **UAE** | Not legislated; labor law governs working hours | No right-to-disconnect requirement, but limits on working hours apply. After-hours work should be compensated or time-off in lieu provided. |
| **India** | Not legislated; draft guidelines exist | No mandatory requirement, but voluntary adoption is strongly recommended given extreme work-hour culture. The company's India policy should actively protect employee rest time. |
| **Brazil** | Not separately legislated; Constitution and CLT govern working hours | No right-to-disconnect requirement, but employer cannot require work outside agreed hours without compensation. Policy should align with statutory limits. |
| **Philippines** | Not legislated; Department of Labor guidelines on flexible work arrangements exist | No mandatory right-to-disconnect, but policy should respect working hour norms. |
| **Canada** | Provincial variation; Quebec legislated (2023); others follow common law | Quebec employees have a statutory right to refuse work communications outside working hours. All Canadian employees should be covered by policy as a minimum standard. |

### The Policy Standard

Regardless of legal requirements, the company adopts the following as its global standard:

1. **Working hours are defined.** Every employee's working hours are defined in their employment contract or a written addendum. The employee is not expected to work outside these hours.

2. **Communication expectations are defined.** Every team establishes a **collaboration agreement** that specifies:
   - Core overlap hours when all team members are available (Tier 1 core hours)
   - Expected response times for different types of communication during working hours
   - After-hours communication protocol (what requires immediate response, what can wait, what does not require response)
   - On-call rotation (if applicable)

3. **After-hours communication is the exception, not the rule.** Managers who send communications outside an employee's defined working hours must do so with the understanding that a response is not required until the employee's next working day, unless the communication is explicitly marked urgent.

4. **Employees may disconnect without notice.** No employee is required to provide advance notice before exercising their right to disconnect. Declining to respond to after-hours communication is not a performance concern.

5. **Time sovereignty is respected.** The company does not require employees to track their non-working time or to seek approval for how they spend time outside working hours.

### Addressing Cultural Pressure

Right-to-disconnect laws address the legal dimension, but cultural pressure operates independently of law. In markets like Japan, South Korea, India, and the Philippines, after-hours work communication may be culturally expected even when legally restricted. The policy addresses this through:

- **Team-level agreements:** Teams, not individuals, set their own after-hours communication norms within the global policy boundaries. This distributes the social pressure and makes norm-setting a collective act.
- **Manager training:** Managers are specifically trained on the right-to-disconnect policy and its interaction with cultural expectations. Managers who model after-hours communication discipline are the most effective compliance mechanism.
- **Anonymous pulse surveys:** Regular surveys ask employees whether they feel pressure to work outside their defined hours. Results are reviewed by HR and regional leadership. Persistent cultural pressure triggers targeted intervention.
- **Leadership modeling:** Regional managing directors and senior leaders are expected to model disconnection publicly. If the managing director sends emails at midnight, the policy is undermined regardless of its legal status.

## V. Addressing the Career-Damage Perception

One of the most significant risks in this policy is that **reduced office presence will be perceived as reduced commitment**, particularly in markets where visible presence has historically been a proxy for dedication. This risk is not hypothetical—it is the primary mechanism through which flexible work policies fail to deliver equitable outcomes.

The company must actively counteract this perception because it is the mechanism through which flexibility becomes available to some employees (typically younger, often male, often without caregiving responsibilities) and unavailable to others (typically women, caregivers, employees from high-presence cultural backgrounds who feel they cannot afford the risk).

### Concrete Measures

**1. Performance system redesign.** The company's performance management system must explicitly decouple visibility from performance:

- Performance review forms remove any field or criterion that captures attendance, presence, or hours worked
- Calibration sessions include a question: "Would this employee's evaluation change if they worked fully remotely?" If the answer is yes, the evaluation is not outcome-based
- Promotion panels receive a diversity report showing promotion rates by flexible work arrangement status; significant disparities trigger review

**2. Manager accountability.** Managers whose teams show promotion rate disparities correlated with flexible work uptake are required to review their own evaluation practices. This is not punitive; it is diagnostic. The goal is to identify and correct unconscious bias.

**3. Sponsorship program.** Employees on Tier 2, 3, or 4 arrangements are paired with senior sponsors who advocate for their career development. The sponsor's role is to ensure that remote or flexible employees are visible for stretch assignments, promotion opportunities, and high-profile projects. This directly addresses the "out of sight, out of mind" problem.

**4. Career path transparency.** The company publishes data (anonymized at the individual level) showing promotion rates, salary progression, and project assignment rates for employees on different work arrangements. If flexible work is genuinely neutral for career outcomes, the data will show this. If it is not, the data will reveal where intervention is needed.

**5. Senior leader visibility.** Senior leaders who work flexibly (including compressed weeks) are publicly identified. Their visibility models the message that flexibility and career advancement are compatible.

## VI. Role-Based Eligibility

Not all roles are equally compatible with all policy tiers. The following framework provides consistent, transparent criteria for eligibility determination.

### Role Categories

| Category | Description | Typical Tier Availability |
|----------|-------------|--------------------------|
| **Category A: Client-Facing, Timezone-Dependent** | Sales, account management, professional services, customer support with real-time client interaction | Tier 1 and 2 only (most roles). Tier 3 only with explicit client communication and coverage arrangements. Tier 4 not available. |

| **Category C: Location-Dependent** | Hardware lab, facilities, office services, security, on-site events | Tier 1 only (flexible hours). Location-dependent roles cannot access Tier 2, 3, or 4. However, these employees receive additional benefits (technology allowance, transport support) to ensure equity. |
| **Category D: Leadership** | People managers at director level and above | All tiers available. Senior leaders are expected to model flexible work behavior and to ensure their teams have access to the full range of options. |

### Eligibility Determination Process

1. **Role self-assessment:** Employees review the role category and available tiers for their role type.
2. **Manager discussion:** Employee and manager discuss preferences, role requirements, and team dynamics.
3. **Manager recommendation:** Manager makes a recommendation based on role suitability and team coverage capacity.
4. **HR review:** HR reviews for consistency, equity, and legal compliance.
5. **Formal arrangement:** Approved arrangements are documented in writing, including the specific tier, any modifications, the review period, and the performance metrics against which the arrangement will be evaluated.
6. **Trial period:** All new arrangements (except Tier 1, which is the default) include a six-month trial period with a structured review.

## VII. Client Expectations Management

A flexible work policy that creates poor client experience will not survive. The company must manage client expectations alongside employee expectations.

### Principles for Client-Facing Flexibility

1. **Client service takes precedence over individual flexibility.** No employee's flexible arrangement excuses them from meeting client commitments. When client needs conflict with individual flexibility, the individual flexibility is adjusted, not the client experience.

2. **Coverage is non-negotiable.** Every client-facing team must maintain coverage during all agreed service hours. This is a team obligation, not an individual obligation. Teams on compressed weeks must arrange internal coverage or adjust client commitments.

3. **Client communication is proactive.** Before implementing a compressed week or location change that affects client availability, the team communicates the new arrangement to affected clients with sufficient notice. Clients should experience continuity, not surprise.

4. **Tier 3 is not available for roles where client expectation of real-time availability is incompatible with the arrangement.** If a client's contract specifies availability outside core hours, Tier 3 is not available for the role without client agreement to modify the contract.

### Commercial Risk Management

- Revenue-generating roles (sales, professional services) that move to Tier 3 should be measured for impact on client satisfaction, deal velocity, and revenue generation before the arrangement is made permanent.
- If data shows measurable client service degradation under a flexible arrangement, the arrangement is modified or revoked.
- Client feedback on flexible arrangements is incorporated into annual policy reviews.

## X. Addressing the Four-Day Week Specifically

Given that four-day week pilots are explicitly mentioned as a demand driver in the scenario, this section addresses four-day weeks with specific attention to the evidence from global pilots conducted between 2022 and 2025.

### What the Evidence Shows

**Successful pilots shared common characteristics:**

- **Role fit:** Success concentrated in roles with clear output metrics, limited real-time client demands, and controlled meeting loads. Engineering, software development, and internal support functions showed the strongest results.
- **Process improvement, not just hour reduction:** The most successful pilots required teams to eliminate low-value work (unnecessary meetings, redundant reports, inefficient workflows) alongside hour reduction. Simply working the same amount of work in fewer hours produced burnout and failure.
- **Collaborative redesign:** Teams that designed their own four-day week arrangements—deciding which day to take off, how to cover meetings, and how to restructure workflows—outperformed teams that received top-down mandates.
- **Trial structure:** All successful pilots used defined trial periods with pre-agreed success metrics and review checkpoints.

**Pilots that struggled or reverted:**

- Roles with high client interaction in markets where four-day weeks are not the norm (clients continued to expect five-day availability)
- Implementation without process improvement (burnout from compressed workload)
- Top-down implementation without team buy-in
- Roles where the nature of the work is inherently time-unstructured (some types of sales, complex project work, crisis management)

### The Company's Approach to Four-Day Weeks

1. **Offer Tier 3 as a trial, not a permanent change.** Six-month trials with defined success criteria. Continuation is data-driven, not automatic.

2. **Require process improvement as a condition.** Teams entering Tier 3 must demonstrate that they have identified and eliminated or restructured at least three low-value activities before reducing hours. This is a team commitment, not an individual one.

3. **Phase by role type.** Launch Tier 3 first in Category B roles (engineering, product, internal operations) where the evidence is strongest. Expand to Category A (client-facing) only after demonstrating client communication protocols that maintain service quality.

4. **Geographic phasing.** Launch in markets where four-day weeks are most culturally and legally compatible (UK, Ireland, Netherlands, Spain). Expand to other markets as evidence accumulates and legal frameworks develop.

5. **Compensation transparency.** Four-day weeks at standard hours (compressed) carry no compensation change. Four-day weeks at reduced hours (80%) carry proportionate compensation adjustment. This must be communicated clearly and consistently.

6. **Equity monitoring.** Track who takes four-day weeks and who does not. If uptake is disproportionately male, younger, or concentrated in specific functions, investigate and address the structural barriers (team coverage pressure, cultural expectations, manager bias).

## A Culturally Adaptive, Legally Compliant, and Operationally Sustainable Policy for a Global Software Company

## Executive Summary

The premise of this policy is straightforward: a one-size-fits-all approach to flexible work will fail in a global organization where employees in one market experience compressed weeks as liberation and employees in another market experience the same arrangement as career-limiting or disloyal. The challenge is not merely logistical—it is cultural, legal, and managerial. What "flexibility" means, what "commitment" signals, and what "visibility" earns differs systematically across the twelve country offices in ways that reflect not employee preference alone but deeply held beliefs about professional reciprocity, organizational loyalty, and the social contract between employer and employee.

This policy does not resolve those differences by imposing a single definition. Instead, it establishes a **global framework of principles and boundaries** within which each regional office adapts the policy to its legal environment, cultural context, and operational requirements. The framework prioritizes outcome-based performance management, legally compliant working-time arrangements, and managerial capability as the primary enablers of sustainable flexibility.

The policy is designed for implementation from 2026 onward, in an environment where **right-to-disconnect legislation has proliferated unevenly** across the company's markets, four-day work week pilots have generated instructive but context-dependent results, and employee expectations—particularly among younger cohorts—have shifted toward flexibility as a significant employment condition.

## I. Policy Architecture: The Core Tension

### The Fundamental Problem

The company faces a three-axis tension:

**Axis 1: Visibility vs. Autonomy.** In some cultural contexts—particularly in high-trust, results-oriented environments—the amount of time an employee spends at a desk or in an office is irrelevant. What matters is whether the work gets done. In other contexts, physical presence signals commitment, diligence, and respect. An employee who leaves the office at 5:00 PM in a high-presence culture may be perceived as a poor performer regardless of output quality. Compressed weeks and remote work, in this context, are not liberating; they are threatening.

**Axis 2: Generational Expectation vs. Established Norm.** Younger employees in markets where four-day week pilots have been publicized—particularly in Northern Europe, parts of Asia-Pacific, and English-speaking markets with strong labor movements—view flexibility as a baseline expectation. In other markets, employees who have built careers on visible dedication may view flexibility policies as benefiting younger employees at their expense, or as an implicit criticism of the career-long sacrifices they made.

**Axis 3: Legal Mandate vs. Operational Desire.** Right-to-disconnect laws in some markets legally restrict after-hours communication; in others, no such laws exist and after-hours availability is culturally expected or contractually implied. Four-day work week pilots have produced legislation in some jurisdictions while remaining experimental in others. The company cannot apply the most restrictive standard globally without constraining operations, but it cannot ignore legal minimums in any market.

### Design Principle

This policy resolves the tension through **regional calibration within global boundaries**, not through compromise across all markets. The company will not choose between a generous policy that fails in high-presence markets and a restrictive policy that fails in autonomy-seeking markets. Instead, it will establish a range of acceptable configurations, each compliant with local law and adapted to local culture, that share common philosophical commitments.

### Scope of Application

This policy applies to all full-time and part-time employees of the company and its wholly owned subsidiaries across its twelve country offices. It does not apply to:

- Contractors and contingent workers, who are governed by their own engagement terms and applicable local law
- Employees in probationary periods, who are subject to the Modified Eligibility provisions in Section VIII
- Seconded employees, who remain subject to the policies of their home country office

Franchisee employees are not covered by this policy. Each franchisee's workforce is governed by local franchise agreement terms and applicable local law, subject to the company's brand standards.

## II. Global Principles

These principles apply in all twelve country offices without exception. They are not negotiable at the regional level, but their implementation is.

### Principle 1: Outcome Primacy

Performance is evaluated on the basis of **delivered outputs, collaboration effectiveness, and professional development**, not on hours logged, physical presence, or visible busyness. Managers in all markets are accountable for evaluating performance on these terms, and performance management systems must be calibrated accordingly.

**What this requires globally:**

- All job descriptions include outcome-based success criteria that are specific, measurable, and independent of attendance or location
- Performance reviews assess outputs against agreed objectives, not presence or hours
- Promotion criteria are explicitly tied to delivery, collaboration quality, and professional growth—not office attendance, availability outside hours, or visible effort
- Managers are trained and held accountable for evaluating performance on outcome criteria, and this competency is assessed in manager performance reviews

**Performance management mechanisms:**

- Quarterly objectives are defined in terms of deliverables, not activities
- 360-degree feedback includes questions about collaboration quality, not availability patterns
- Calibration sessions include a structured review of whether remote or flexible employees receive equivalent recognition to on-site peers
- Compensation decisions (merit increases, bonuses, equity awards) are audited for correlation with flexibility arrangement type; any statistically significant disparity triggers a review of the decision-making process

### Principle 2: Legal Floor

No regional policy may fall below the legal minimum standards of the relevant jurisdiction. This includes working time limits, mandatory rest periods, right-to-disconnect protections, overtime rules, notice requirements for schedule changes, and any requirements for collective bargaining or works council consultation.

**What this requires globally:**

- Legal review of all regional policy variants before implementation, conducted by local counsel in each jurisdiction
- Annual legal compliance audit for each country office, with findings reported to the Global Flexibility Working Group
- A legal compliance matrix maintained centrally and updated within 60 days of any material change in legislation
- Clear escalation path for employees who believe their rights are being violated, operating independently of the normal management chain to ensure protection against retaliation
- Ongoing legislative monitoring through a designated legal resource in each market

### Principle 3: Team Accountability

Individual flexibility exists within the context of team obligations. Flexibility is not unlimited discretion—it is structured autonomy exercised within team commitments, client service requirements, and collaborative workflows.

**What this requires globally:**

- Team-level agreements that define collaboration windows, overlap hours, and meeting attendance expectations, developed collaboratively by each team within global parameters
- Clear identification of role-specific requirements (client-facing hours, time-zone coverage, availability during core business hours) before any flexibility arrangement is approved
- Team accountability mechanisms that make flexibility visible as a collective arrangement, not an individual perk
- Manager authority to set team-level parameters within the global framework and to revoke flexibility arrangements that systematically undermine team obligations, subject to appeal

### Principle 4: Managerial Capability as Prerequisite

Flexible work arrangements are only as effective as the managers who implement them. Managers who cannot set clear expectations, provide constructive feedback, manage performance across distance, and support team collaboration in a flexible environment will undermine any policy, regardless of its design.

**What this requires globally:**

- Manager certification program, completed before teams under a manager's supervision are eligible for Tier 2, Tier 3, or Tier 4 arrangements
- Ongoing manager development on outcome-based performance management, delivered annually
- Manager performance evaluation incorporating team flexibility management effectiveness as a rated competency
- Resources (training, coaching, peer support) for managers operating in mixed-attendance or fully-remote teams, available on demand
- Manager certification covers: outcome-based objective setting, performance conversations without presence cues, managing distributed teams, preventing proximity bias, handling flexibility exceptions, right-to-disconnect enforcement, and cultural awareness for managing cross-border teams

### Principle 5: Equity, Not Equality

The policy aims for equitable access to flexibility across demographics, roles, and seniority levels—not identical treatment, which would be neither equitable nor operationally sensible. Certain roles cannot be performed flexibly (facilities staff, hardware lab technicians, security personnel); the policy addresses these role-specific constraints directly rather than ignoring them.

Equitable access means that the barriers to flexibility are objective (role requirements, legal constraints, operational needs) rather than discretionary (manager preference, cultural norm, seniority-based privilege). The company monitors uptake and outcome data to identify where discretionary barriers are distorting equitable access.

## III. The Policy Options: Four Tiers

Rather than offering a single "flexible work policy," this framework defines **four tiers of flexibility**, each with associated eligibility criteria, structural requirements, and regional customization parameters. Not all tiers are available in all markets; availability depends on role suitability, legal compliance, and regional adoption readiness.

### Tier 1: Flexible Hours (Default)

**Core provision:** Employees may vary their start and end times within a defined core window, subject to team collaboration requirements. Tier 1 is the baseline policy for all eligible employees; it requires no formal application process.

| Parameter | Standard Configuration | Regional Customization Range |
|-----------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| **Core hours (all employees must be available)** | 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM local time | 9:00 AM – 2:00 PM to 11:00 AM – 4:00 PM, adjusted for local norms |
| **Working day length** | Standard full-time hours per local contract (e.g., 8 hours) | May be reduced to 7.5 hours with manager approval in markets where cultural norms and legal frameworks support shorter standard days |
| **Right-to-disconnect boundary** | After 6:00 PM local time, no expectation of response unless on-call or on duty roster | Legally mandated boundaries take precedence; where no law exists, 6:00 PM is the default |
| **Location** | Office-based; no remote work requirement or restriction under this tier | — |
| **Meeting attendance** | Expected during core hours; may decline non-essential meetings outside core hours with reasonable notice | — |
| **Overtime** | Time off in lieu or compensation per local law for hours worked beyond contractual daily hours | Per local legal requirements |

**Regional calibration examples:**

- *Germany:* Core window 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM. Works council (Betriebsrat) consultation and co-determination rights apply to any core-hour modification affecting the workforce. Right-to-disconnect is not separately legislated but is established through labor court precedent and the General Data Protection Regulation's right to restriction of processing. Works council can negotiate works agreements (Betriebsvereinbarungen) on the topic.
- *Japan:* Core window may be extended to 11:00 AM – 4:00 PM given cultural expectations around arrival time. However, after-hours communication culture remains strong; team agreements should explicitly address after-hours norms rather than relying on the right-to-disconnect boundary alone.
- *Brazil:* Core window of 9:00 AM – 3:00 PM, with overtime governed by CLT provisions. Brazilian law caps the standard workday at 8 hours and the standard work week at 44 hours. - *Singapore:* Core window 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM; no statutory right-to-disconnect. The Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangements (updated 2024) recommend employer flexibility but do not mandate it. Team norms govern after-hours communication, which tends to be higher than in European markets. Managers should explicitly negotiate after-hours expectations rather than assuming availability.
- *India:* Core window 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM IST. The Factories Act and state Shops and Establishments Acts govern working hours; standard workday is 9 hours including a break. Right-to-disconnect is not legislated, but the Code on Wages (2019) and proposed labor reforms establish limits on working hours. The company's India policy should explicitly protect rest time given the cultural prevalence of extended working hours.
- *UAE:* Core window 9:00 AM – 3:00 PM given reduced Friday hours and Ramadan adjustments. UAE Labour Law caps the standard workday at 8 hours and working week at 48 hours. After-hours work should be compensated with time off in lieu or additional pay per statutory requirements. Right-to-disconnect is not legislated.

**Eligibility:** All full-time and part-time employees in roles that do not require physical presence at a specific location or shift coverage are eligible for Tier 1. This is the default; employees do not need to apply.

- Ensure that career advancement decisions are not influenced by an employee's physical presence in ways that contradict Principle 1

### Tier 3: Compressed or Reduced Work Week

**Core provision:** Employees may restructure their working week to concentrate standard hours into fewer days, or may reduce total hours with corresponding compensation adjustment. Tier 3 requires formal application, manager recommendation, HR approval, and a six-month trial with defined outcome metrics.

| Option | Configuration | Regional Availability |
|--------|--------------|----------------------|
| **Four-day week (compressed: standard hours in four days)** | Work standard weekly hours Monday–Thursday, with Friday off | Available where legally permitted and operationally feasible for the role. Not available in roles where five-day real-time availability is contractually or operationally required. |
| **Four-day week (reduced: 32 hours at 80% compensation)** | Work 32 hours (80% of standard) for 80% of base compensation | Available where legally permitted. Requires explicit manager and HR approval and a six-month trial with review. Benefits and equity vesting pro-rated accordingly. |
| **Nine-day fortnight** | Work standard hours across nine days every two weeks, with every other Friday off | Available in most markets. Appeals to markets where employees appreciate variety over rigid schedule changes. |
| **Job share** | Two employees share a full-time role, each working part-time | Available globally. Requires role suitability assessment, formal job-share agreement, and configuration review to ensure coverage. |

**Compensation principles for Tier 3:**

- **Compressed (full hours, fewer days):** No change to base compensation. The employee works the same total hours in fewer days. This is the preferred option for four-day weeks because it maintains pay equity.
- **Reduced (fewer hours, proportionally less pay):** Compensation is reduced proportionally to hours. This is appropriate when the reduction is substantial and sustained, not merely seasonal.
- **Proportionality review:** If a reduced-hours arrangement is combined with a role change (e.g., moving from a senior role to a reduced-scope role), compensation adjustment may exceed the proportional hours reduction. HR determines this on a case-by-case basis.
- **Benefits:** Benefits that are tied to hours (e.g., accrual-based leave) are adjusted proportionally. Benefits that are not tied to hours (health insurance, equity) remain unchanged unless legally required otherwise.

**Eligibility criteria for Tier 3:**

- Minimum 12 months of service (excluding probationary period)
- Current performance rating of "meets expectations" or above
- Role categorized as Category B (Collaborative, Outcome-Oriented) or specifically approved by HR on exception
- Manager certification completed
- Team coverage plan documented and approved
- Client impact assessment completed (for client-facing roles)
- Trial objectives and metrics agreed in writing before commencement

**What the evidence tells us about four-day weeks:**

Global pilots conducted between 2022 and 2025—including Iceland's national trial (2015–2019), the UK's largest four-day week pilot (2022, 61 companies, 2,900 employees), Unilever's partnership with the Productivity Institute (2023), and pilot programs in Australia, Canada, Japan, and South Africa—consistently demonstrated that:

1. **Role fit is the strongest predictor of success.** Roles with clear output metrics, controlled meeting loads, and limited real-time client demands showed the strongest results. Software development, engineering, internal operations, and analytical roles performed well. Client-facing sales, professional services, and roles with high crisis management demands showed more variable results.

2. **Process improvement is a prerequisite, not an accompaniment.** The most successful pilots required teams to eliminate or restructure low-value work alongside hour reduction. Simply compressing the same workload into fewer hours produced burnout, quality degradation, or informal after-hours work that defeated the purpose.

3. **Collaborative design outperforms top-down mandates.** Teams that designed their own arrangements—deciding which day to take off, how to cover meetings, how to restructure workflows—consistently outperformed those receiving standardized prescriptions.

4. **Sustained results require cultural change, not just schedule change.** Many pilots showed initial enthusiasm that faded as the novelty wore off and the underlying work culture reasserted itself. Organizations that treated four-day weeks as a scheduling change alone had higher reversion rates than those that treated it as part of a broader cultural shift.

5. **The 100-80-100 model (100% of pay for 80% of time in exchange for 100% of productivity) showed the strongest results in terms of employee wellbeing and retention, though revenue impact was mixed.**

**Regional calibration examples:**

- *UK:* Four-day week is legally available. Several pilots have been conducted by major employers (including some technology companies). Market expectation is that compressed four-day weeks maintain full output; reduced-hours four-day weeks require explicit compensation adjustment. Tier 3 should be presented as an earned privilege tied to team performance and individual track record, not an entitlement.
- *Spain:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible and supported by Spain's progressive labor reforms. - *Germany:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible as a working time arrangement. - *France:* Four-day weeks are legally permissible. Younger employees in tech and startup environments have expressed strong interest, but uptake is likely to be gradual.

Tier 3 in the Philippines should include explicit protections against informal pressure to work on days off.

- Every team on Tier 3 arrangements must have coverage during the reduced employee's working day. This is the manager's responsibility to arrange, not the employee's.
- Tier 3 arrangements that leave critical functions uncovered are not approved. "Critical function" is defined jointly by the manager and HR.
- Where coverage cannot be arranged sustainably, Tier 3 is not available for that role until coverage is resolved.
- Coverage arrangements are reviewed at each trial checkpoint.

### Tier 4: Remote-First (Full Flexibility)

**Core provision:** Employees may work entirely remotely with no required in-office presence, subject to periodic in-person requirements for strategic purposes.

| Parameter | Configuration |
|-----------|--------------|
| **Location** | Employee's country of employment; cross-border remote requires separate international remote work agreement, which triggers tax, social security, and employment law analysis in the destination country |
| **In-person requirements** | Minimum 4 weeks per year for team strategic planning, culture events, or mandatory in-person activities. In-person requirements are planned at least 8 weeks in advance. |
| **Equipment** | Company-provided equipment; enhanced home office stipend |
| **Right-to-disconnect** | Legally mandated boundaries apply; where no law exists, the policy default applies |
| **Eligibility** | Role-suitability assessed; manager recommendation; HR and Legal review; six-month trial period |

**Tier 4 availability is not universal.** Availability is determined on a country-by-country basis after legal and tax review, because:

- Remote workers in a foreign country may create a **permanent establishment** for the company, triggering corporate tax obligations
- Remote workers may create **employment law obligations** in their country of residence that differ from their country of employment
- Remote workers may become subject to **social security contributions** in their country of residence
- The company may be required to **withhold taxes** according to the rules of the remote worker's country of residence

**Countries where Tier 4 is likely available with manageable legal complexity:** UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia (with Fair Work compliance), Netherlands, Sweden, Spain.

**Countries where Tier 4 requires significant legal review or is inadvisable due to permanent establishment risk:** Japan, South Korea, India, UAE, Singapore.

**Countries where Tier 4 is legally complex but potentially manageable:** Germany (works council negotiation required; permanent establishment risk must be assessed), France (cadres on forfait jours may be eligible; cross-border remote requires careful structuring), Brazil (employment law complexity, tax implications, and CLT obligations must be assessed per state).

**Tier 4 is not a right.** It is an earned arrangement that requires:

- Successful completion of a Tier 2 or Tier 3 arrangement, or explicit HR waiver for roles that bypass Tier 2/3 due to specific circumstances
- Consistent delivery against outcome-based performance criteria for at least two consecutive review periods
- Demonstration of effective independent collaboration
- Manager recommendation with documented rationale
- HR and Legal review confirming no legal or tax complications
- Six-month trial period with defined performance metrics

### The Policy Standard

Regardless of legal requirements, the company adopts the following as its global standard:

1. **Working hours are defined.** Every employee's working hours are defined in their employment contract or a written addendum. The employee is not expected to work outside these hours.

2. **Communication expectations are defined.** Every team establishes a **collaboration agreement** within 30 days of formation or policy adoption, specifying:
   - Core overlap hours when all team members are available (Tier 1 core hours)
   - Expected response times for different types of communication during working hours (e.g., email: within 4 hours during core hours; instant messages: within 1 hour during core hours; project management tools: within one working day)
   - After-hours communication protocol (what requires immediate response, what can wait, what does not require response)
   - On-call rotation (if applicable)
   - How urgent escalation is initiated and who authorizes it

3. **After-hours communication is the exception, not the rule.** Managers who send communications outside an employee's defined working hours must do so with the understanding that a response is not required until the employee's next working day, unless the communication is explicitly marked urgent and includes a brief justification for the urgency. The word "urgent" should not be used routinely; its repeated misuse is addressed through manager coaching.

4. **Employees may disconnect without notice.** No employee is required to provide advance notice before exercising their right to disconnect. Declining to respond to after-hours communication is not a performance concern and must not be referenced in performance evaluations.

5. **Time sovereignty is respected.** The company does not require employees to track their non-working time or to seek approval for how they spend time outside working hours.

6. **Monitoring software is limited.** The company does not deploy software that monitors employee activity outside working hours or that could be used to infer whether an employee is working during their stated working hours. Time-tracking software, where used, records hours worked, not activity levels during working hours.

### Addressing Cultural Pressure

Right-to-disconnect laws address the legal dimension, but cultural pressure operates independently of law. In markets like Japan, South Korea, India, and the Philippines, after-hours work communication may be culturally expected even when legally restricted. The policy addresses this through:

- **Team-level agreements:** Teams, not individuals, set their own after-hours communication norms within the global policy boundaries. This distributes the social pressure and makes norm-setting a collective act. Teams should revisit their agreements at least annually.
- **Manager training:** Managers are specifically trained on the right-to-disconnect policy, its interaction with cultural expectations, and how to manage the gap between formal policy and cultural practice. This training includes practical scenarios: what to do when a client sends an after-hours email, how to support a team member who is experiencing cultural pressure to overwork, how to model disconnection publicly.

#### Leadership modeling

Senior leaders are expected to model disconnection publicly. If the Managing Director sends emails at midnight, the policy is undermined regardless of its legal status. Senior leaders should:

- Set their own email delivery schedules to respect right-to-disconnect boundaries
- Communicate publicly when they take time off
- Respond to after-hours messages from their teams with explicit acknowledgment that no response is expected until working hours
- Participate in manager training alongside their teams

#### Anonymous pulse surveys

Regular pulse surveys ask employees whether they feel pressure to work outside their defined hours. The survey design is critical: asking employees directly whether they experience pressure is less effective than asking behavioral questions (e.g., "How often do you respond to work communications outside your defined working hours?"). Behavioral questions are more accurate and less subject to social desirability bias. Results are reviewed by HR and regional leadership quarterly. Persistent cultural pressure triggers targeted intervention, which may include manager coaching, team norm renegotiation, or escalation to regional leadership.

#### Safe reporting mechanism

Employees who experience pressure to work outside their hours and feel unable to raise it with their manager have access to a confidential reporting channel, operated by HR Business Partners independent of the reporting employee's management chain. This channel is distinct from the anonymous pulse survey and allows for individual follow-up.
